blogs.title: The Perils of a 'Pivoting' Expert: Technical Testimony and the Substantial Evidence Standard
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Federal Circuit’s decision to reverse a jury verdict based on an expert witness’s self-contradictory testimony. It explores the legal implications of 'pivoting' testimony in complex technical fields, specifically how the court treats a plaintiff's failure to maintain a consistent mapping of technology to claim limitations. The discussion will focus on the 'substantial evidence' standard and what this means for the evidentiary burden of the plaintiff in high-tech patent litigation.

blogs.title: Prosecution History and the 'Unique Signal' Trap: Navigating Claim Scope in Signal Processing
blogs.description: Focusing on the '775 patent, this post examines the nuances of claim construction regarding 'separately identifiable' versus 'unique' signals. It will delve into the court's analysis of whether a patentee’s amendment to 'three signals' during prosecution constitutes a disavowal of products using only 'two signals.' The post will discuss the broader implications for how practitioners must balance claim breadth against prosecution history estoppel in technical hardware patents.

blogs.title: When Mathematics Fails the Mapping Test: The Stricture of Specific Claim Limitations
blogs.description: This post explores the Federal Circuit’s treatment of specific mathematical and numerical limitations within a patent claim—in this case, the requirement for seven specific multiplications. It analyzes the court's finding that even if a device performs similar functions, a failure to provide a clear, explicit 'mapping' between the accused product's operations and the patent's exact mathematical requirements can lead to a JMOL of noninfringement. This highlights a critical hurdle for plaintiffs in cases involving complex algorithm-based hardware.
